title: What a switch is, and the frame it reads
summary: A switch is a Layer 2 device whose entire job is to move Ethernet frames between ports using MAC addresses. To reason about it, you need the frame fields it actually looks at.

sections.heading: Ethernet frames: only four fields matter for switching
sections.html:
A frame on the wire is bytes, not a diagram, but the fields a switch reads are these:

+------------------+------------------+-----------+---------------------+-----+| dst MAC (6 bytes) | src MAC (6 bytes) | 802.1Q?   | EtherType (2 bytes) | ... |+------------------+------------------+-----------+---------------------+-----+| FCS (4 bytes) at the very end                                    |
FieldWhy the switch cares
Destination MACLookup key for the forwarding decision
Source MACLookup key for learning
Optional 802.1Q tagVLAN membership on a trunk
EtherTypeUsually ignored for forwarding; tells the receiver whether it is IPv4 (0x0800), IPv6 (0x86DD), ARP (0x0806) or 802.1Q (0x8100)

The minimum frame is 64 bytes including FCS; smaller frames are runts and are discarded. Maximum payload is 1500 bytes by default (MTU), so the maximum frame is 1518 bytes — 1522 with a VLAN tag. MTU is a Layer 3 concern, but oversized frames are dropped at Layer 2, which is why 'ping works, big transfers stall' often points at MTU or a broken path MTU discovery.

sections.heading: MAC addresses are flat, and that shapes the switch
sections.html:
A MAC is 48 bits: 24 bits OUI (vendor) plus 24 bits assigned by the vendor. It is flat — there is no hierarchy and therefore no way to summarise a range of MACs. IP is hierarchical, which is why routers can hold a routing table with a few hundred thousand entries while switches must learn individual addresses.

Two consequences:

  • Switches must learn per-address, which is why MAC tables have finite size and overflow into flooding.
  • MAC addresses have no location meaning. A MAC in VLAN 10 says nothing about VLAN 20; that is why broadcast domains are enforced separately by VLAN membership.

Also worth knowing: 01:00:5e:... and 33:33:... are multicast; ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff is broadcast; the second-least-significant bit of the first octet marks locally administered addresses (common with virtualisation).

sections.heading: Switch versus hub versus router
sections.html:
HubSwitchRouter
Layer123
Forwards byNothing — repeats bits to all portsDestination MACDestination IP / routing table
Collision domainOne shared domainOne per port (full duplex)One per port
Broadcast domainOneOne per VLANSeparate per interface by default
Blocks broadcasts?NoNo (only separates VLANs)Yes

The historical collision-domain point matters in interviews: with hubs, CSMA/CD managed shared media and every host heard every frame. Switches removed the shared medium, so collision domains became per-port and CSMA/CD is effectively obsolete on switched full-duplex links. Broadcast domains did not disappear with switches — they moved to VLAN boundaries.

Common misconception: 'A switch breaks up broadcast domains.' It does not, unless you configure VLANs. A 48-port switch with one VLAN is one broadcast domain with 48 collision domains.

checks.prompt: Which statement about collision and broadcast domains on a single VLAN is correct?
options: One collision domain and one broadcast domain
One collision domain and one broadcast domain per port
One collision domain per port and one broadcast domain
One collision domain per port and one broadcast domain per port
checks.explanation: A switch gives each port its own collision domain (full duplex, no shared medium) but the whole VLAN remains one broadcast domain.

why_wrong.1: Broadcast domains are per-VLAN, not per-port.
why_wrong.3: That would mean every port is isolated, which only happens with port isolation features.

checks.prompt: A frame arrives with destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. What does the switch do?
options: Floods it to every port in the VLAN except the ingress port
Sends it only to the port where that MAC was learned
checks.explanation: The all-ones destination is broadcast, so it must reach every station in the broadcast domain.

why_wrong.2: There is no table entry for a broadcast address to learn.
why_wrong.3: Broadcasts are valid and essential for ARP and DHCP.
why_wrong.1: Switches do not forward broadcasts to a router by default.

connect.title: ARP
connect.text: ARP requests are broadcasts — they are flooded exactly as this lesson describes, which is why a large flat VLAN gets noisy.

connect.title: IP addressing
connect.text: A VLAN should map one-to-one with a subnet. Mismatched VLAN/subnet design is a classic source of one-way communication.

connect.title: Routing
connect.text: Routers terminate broadcast domains. The first router hop is where intra-VLAN switching ends and IP forwarding begins.

interview.q: What is the difference between a switch and a router?
interview.a: A switch forwards frames within a Layer 2 broadcast domain using MAC addresses learned from traffic; it does not decrement TTL or rewrite IP. A router forwards packets between Layer 3 networks using the destination IP and a routing table, decrements TTL, rewrites the link-layer header per hop, and terminates broadcasts.

interview.q: Why does a switch need a MAC table at all?
interview.a: Because MAC addresses are flat, there is no summary or hierarchy the switch can use to infer a location. It must learn which interface each address is reachable through, and flood when it does not know.
